title: Polymer clay faux wood grain pendant
subtitle: A warm oval pendant with realistic wood-grain patterning, baked in a domestic oven
excerpt: A faux wood grain effect in polymer clay uses two tones of brown mixed to a partial blend, then rolled and folded to create parallel grain lines. Sliced into a thin oval and baked, the result reads as polished wood. A hole drilled before baking takes a jump ring for a cord.
sourceNotes: Faux wood-grain technique derived from first principles for polymer clay.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling clay that cures hard in a domestic oven at 110-130°C; decorative, not food-safe
Kneading polymer clay by hand until warm and pliable
A technique for blending two polymer clay colours into a smooth gradient by folding and rolling a two-tone slab repeatedly

content.text: Faux wood grain in
polymer clay
comes from blending two browns to a partial
Skinner blend

, mixed enough to create directional streaks but not so mixed that the colours merge. Rolling in one direction and folding along the grain axis keeps the streaks parallel. The finished pendant is 3-4 cm long.

materials.name: Polymer clay, ochre or cream (optional grain accent)

content.text: Conditioning and blending
Condition
both colours separately until fully warm and pliable.
Form dark brown into a flat slab and light tan into a matching flat slab. Place them side by side with edges touching. Roll once to join them into a single two-tone slab.

Fold the slab in half along the colour boundary , fold dark to dark, tan to tan , and roll again. Repeat this fold-and-roll eight to twelve times. The two colours will form long parallel streaks. Stop before the colours fully merge. The streaks should still be two distinct tones with jagged transition edges between them.
Cutting the pendant shape
Roll the blended slab to 4 mm thick. Cut an oval 4 cm x 3 cm. The grain lines should run along the long axis of the oval , rotate the cutting template to align with the streaks if needed.
Use a needle tool to pierce a hole 3 mm from the top of the oval, centred on the long axis. Twist the needle gently in both directions to clean the hole without distorting the oval.
Baking and finishing
Bake on baking parchment at 130°C for 25 minutes. Allow to cool completely.

Sand the pendant face through fine-grade paper if the surface has any marks, working through 400 grit, 800 grit, and 1200 grit for a polished result. This is optional , a sanded surface looks more like polished wood and takes varnish better.
Apply two coats of gloss acrylic varnish, drying fully between each coat.
Thread a jump ring through the hole and attach to a leather or waxed cord.
Variations
Cut a rectangular shape for a more polished, modern pendant.
Add a thin ochre streak between the two brown layers before folding to mimic the lighter heartwood grain of ash or oak.
Make matching earring discs using 2 cm circles cut from the same blended slab.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Colours merged completely , no grain visible
items.fix: Stop the blending earlier next time. If both colours are already merged, the slab can still be used as a plain brown piece , add a thin layer of contrasting colour on top for a two-tone pendant instead

items.problem: Grain lines run in the wrong direction on the pendant
items.cause: The cutting template was not aligned to the grain direction
items.fix: Check grain direction before cutting and rotate the oval template to match

items.problem: Hole tore the top of the pendant on baking
items.cause: Hole placed too close to the edge
items.fix: Keep the hole at least 4 mm from any edge. Re-pierce a hole slightly lower before baking if the first hole is too close
